items.title: Lithium has a stronger 'urge' to react than sodium — and reacts more gently
items.claim: Drop sodium into water: it fizzes violently, often igniting with a yellow flame. Drop lithium into water: it floats and fizzes calmly. Yet lithium's standard electrode potential (-3.04 V) is MORE negative than sodium's (-2.71 V).
items.prompt: Why doesn't lithium react more vigorously?

options.text: Lithium's high melting point (181°C) means it stays solid during reaction; the LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms a coating that slows further reaction. Sodium melts in the reaction heat and exposes fresh surface
Standard electrode potentials are wrong for lithium
Lithium does not actually react with water

items.reveal:
Lithium's small ion has a very large hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs sodium's -406), which more than compensates for its higher ionisation energy. So thermodynamically it has the highest tendency in Group 1 to lose an electron in aqueous solution.

But reactivity at the bench is rate-controlled by surface kinetics. Sodium melts at 98°C, well below the temperature reached during reaction with water — molten sodium spreads and exposes fresh metal. Lithium melts at 181°C and stays solid.

LiOH solubility is about 12 g per 100 g water; NaOH is 109 g. The lithium product crusts on the surface and slows further attack.
items.why: The reactivity series is taught as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force and a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Ice expands by about 9 percent on freezing
items.claim: Most substances contract on freezing — atoms pack more tightly in solids. Water expands by 9 percent. This is why pipes burst in winter, why icebergs float, and why rocks shatter when water in their cracks freezes.
items.prompt: What forces 'open' the structure of ice?

options.text: Each water molecule in ice forms exactly four directional hydrogen bonds in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement; the geometry produces an open hexagonal lattice with large empty channels
Water molecules grow larger when cold
Ice contains less water than liquid water

items.reveal:
In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and re-form rapidly, and molecules pack close. When water freezes, every molecule locks into a tetrahedral geometry — each oxygen H-bonded to four neighbours at fixed angles.

The geometry produces a hexagonal lattice with significant empty space — about 9 percent more volume than liquid water at the same temperature. So ice has density 0.917 g/cm3 vs liquid water's 1.000 g/cm3.

Freeze-thaw weathering breaks rocks and shapes mountain landscapes. Frost-heave damages roads. Burst pipes flood homes. The 9 percent expansion has shaped half the planet's geology.
items.why: Volume change on freezing is taught as a curiosity. It has huge consequences for biology, geology and civil engineering.

items.title: Pure water dissolves more silver chloride than salt water does
items.claim: Silver chloride is famously insoluble — Ksp is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10. But it dissolves slightly. Try to dissolve it in salt water and the solubility plummets to almost zero.
items.prompt: Why does adding more Cl- decrease AgCl solubility?

options.text: Le Chatelier — adding more Cl- shifts AgCl(s) is in equilibrium with Ag+ + Cl- back to the left, reducing dissolved Ag+ until [Ag+][Cl-] equals Ksp again
Silver chloride decomposes in salt water
Salt water becomes saturated with itself, leaving no room for AgCl

items.reveal:
Suppose in pure water solubility 's' equals square root of Ksp, around 1.3 times 10 to the minus 5 M for AgCl.

In 0.1 M NaCl, [Cl-] is dominated by the salt (about 0.1 M). [Ag+] must satisfy [Ag+] times 0.1 equals 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10, so [Ag+] is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 9 M. Solubility drops by a factor of nearly 10,000.

This is exploited in gravimetric analysis: precipitate the analyte by adding excess of a common ion, ensuring almost everything comes out of solution.
items.why: Students think 'dissolved + dissolved = more dissolved'. Le Chatelier flips the intuition for ionic equilibria.
